content: Corticosteroids are effective in inducing remission in Crohn's disease but are not suitable for maintaining remission due to significant risks of adverse events, especially with prolonged use. Budesonide, a glucocorticoid with limited systemic bioavailability due to extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, has been shown to be effective in inducing remission in Crohn's disease. However, its role in maintaining remission remains unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral budesonide for maintaining remission in Crohn's disease. A systematic search of multiple databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, was conducted up to June 12, 2014. Randomized controlled trials comparing budesonide to placebo, other treatments, or different doses of budesonide were included. The study population consisted of patients with quiescent Crohn's disease. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE criteria. Twelve studies involving 1,273 patients were included. Eight studies compared budesonide to placebo, while others compared it to 5-aminosalicylates, systemic corticosteroids, azathioprine, or different doses of budesonide. Most studies used a controlled ileal release formulation of budesonide, while a few used a pH-modified release formulation. Nine studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while three had a high risk of bias due to issues with blinding and allocation concealment. Budesonide 6 mg daily was not significantly more effective than placebo in maintaining remission at 3, 6, or 12 months. At 3 months, 64% of patients on budesonide remained in remission compared to 52% on placebo (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.58). The quality of evidence for this outcome was low due to moderate heterogeneity and sparse data. At 6 months, 61% of budesonide patients remained in remission compared to 52% on placebo (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.39), with moderate-quality evidence. At 12 months, 55% of budesonide patients remained in remission compared to 48% on placebo (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.35), with moderate-quality evidence. Budesonide 3 mg daily also showed no significant benefit over placebo at 6 and 12 months. There was no significant difference in remission rates at 12 months between budesonide and weaning doses of prednisolone (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.13). The quality of evidence for this comparison was low due to sparse data and high risk of bias. Budesonide 6 mg was more effective than mesalamine 3 g/day at 12 months (RR 2.51, 95% CI 1.03 to 6.12), but the quality of evidence was very low due to sparse data and high risk of bias. No significant difference was observed between budesonide and azathioprine at 12 months (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.08), with very low-quality evidence due to sparse data and high risk of bias. Budesonide 6 mg resulted in slight improvements in Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) scores at 6 months (MD -24.30, 95% CI -46.31 to -2.29) and 12 months (MD -23.49, 95% CI -46.65 to -0.32). It also prolonged the mean time to relapse (MD 59.93 days, 95% CI 19.02 to 100.84). However, the mean time to relapse was shorter for budesonide compared to azathioprine (MD -58.00, 95% CI -96.68 to -19.32). Adverse events were not significantly more common in patients treated with budesonide compared to placebo (6 mg: RR 1.51, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.52; 3 mg: RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.24). These adverse events were generally mild and did not lead to increased study withdrawal rates. Commonly reported side effects included acne, moon facies, hirsutism, mood swings, insomnia, weight gain, striae, and hair loss. However, abnormal adrenocorticoid stimulation tests were more frequent in patients receiving budesonide 6 mg (RR 2.88, 95% CI 1.72 to 4.82) and 3 mg (RR 2.73, 95% CI 1.34 to 5.57) compared to placebo. In conclusion, budesonide is not effective for maintaining remission in Crohn's disease, particularly beyond three months after induction of remission. While it offers minor benefits in terms of lower CDAI scores and longer time to relapse, these are outweighed by the higher rates of treatment-related adverse events and more frequent adrenocorticoid suppression.
